z1-rc1.title: Passage: Libraries of things
z1-rc1.html:
Passage: Libraries of things

Most households own an electric drill, yet the average drill is used for only a few minutes in its whole life. It spends years in a drawer, waiting for the one shelf that needs putting up. The same is true of ladders, pressure washers, camping tents and sewing machines. Each family buys its own, stores its own and eventually throws its own away, often while it still works. Multiply that by every street in a town and the result is a great deal of money, metal and plastic sitting idle in the dark.

A small but growing number of towns have tried a different arrangement: the library of things. It works much like a book library. Members pay a small yearly fee, or nothing at all, and borrow tools and equipment for a few days at a time. A volunteer checks each item when it comes back, charges the batteries and notes any damage. The collection usually starts with donations from people clearing out garages and grows as members suggest what they would like to borrow.

Supporters point to three benefits. The first is money: a family that borrows a carpet cleaner twice a year saves the price of buying one. The second is space, which matters in small city flats where a cupboard is precious. The third is waste. When fewer people buy rarely used items, fewer are made, shipped and finally dumped. Some libraries also run repair evenings, where volunteers show members how to fix a broken toaster instead of replacing it.

The idea has limits. A library of things works best where people live close together, because nobody wants to travel an hour to borrow a hammer. It also depends on trust. If borrowers return items late or broken, the collection shrinks and members drift away. Several early projects closed for exactly this reason. The ones that last tend to keep careful records, ask for a refundable deposit on costly items and, above all, build a sense that the collection belongs to the members rather than to some distant organisation.

Perhaps the most surprising lesson is that the libraries are not only about objects. Members often say that the best part is meeting neighbours they had never spoken to, swapping advice on how to use a tile cutter, or being asked to help with a project. In that sense a shelf of shared tools does what the town square once did: it gives people a reason to meet.

z1-rc2.title: Passage: How a beehive keeps its temperature
z1-rc2.html:
Passage: How a beehive keeps its temperature

A honeybee colony behaves in some ways like a single warm-blooded animal. The developing young bees, or brood, need a steady temperature of about 34 to 35 degrees Celsius. A few degrees too cold and they develop slowly or with defects; a few degrees too hot and they may die. The adult workers therefore spend a great deal of their energy keeping the brood area at just the right warmth, whatever the weather outside. The rest of the hive, where honey and pollen are stored, is allowed to vary much more. The colony, in other words, does not heat or cool its whole home evenly; it protects the part that matters most for its future.

When the air is cold, workers cluster tightly over the brood. Many of them produce heat by rapidly tensing the large flight muscles in their bodies without moving their wings, much as a person shivers. A bee doing this can raise its own body temperature well above that of the air around it. Bees on the outside of the cluster pack closely together and act like an insulating blanket, while those inside generate the warmth. The work is tiring, and bees on the cold outer layer gradually move inwards to warm up while others take their place.

Heat is the opposite problem in summer. Workers line up at the entrance and fan their wings to drive air through the hive. On very hot days others fly out to collect water, spread thin films of it over the comb and fan it so that it evaporates. Evaporation takes heat away, so the hive is cooled in roughly the way a damp cloth cools a clay pot.

No single bee is in charge of any of this. Each worker reacts to the temperature it senses nearby, and individuals seem to differ slightly in the temperature at which they start to fan or to shiver. Because of these small differences, the colony does not swing wildly between all-out heating and all-out cooling. As conditions change, a few bees respond first, then more join in, and the response grows smoothly.

Beekeepers have learned to respect this system. Opening a hive on a cold morning, for instance, can undo hours of careful warming, and a hive placed in full afternoon sun forces the colony to spend its effort fetching water instead of food. Good management, in short, means making the bees' own work easier rather than replacing it.

z1-rc3.title: Passage: Notes by hand and notes by keyboard
z1-rc3.html:
Passage: Notes by hand and notes by keyboard

Students who carry laptops into lectures can type almost as fast as a teacher speaks. Students who write by hand cannot; even a quick writer manages perhaps a third of what is said. At first sight this looks like a clear win for the laptop: more words captured should mean more material to revise from. Yet several classroom studies have suggested that students who take notes by hand often do as well as, or better than, typists on later questions that test understanding.

One explanation lies in the very slowness of handwriting. A student writing by hand cannot copy every sentence, so she has to decide what matters and put it in her own words. That act of choosing and rephrasing forces her to think about the ideas while she hears them. A fast typist, by contrast, can take down the lecture almost word for word without stopping to process it. The notes are longer, but less of the thinking has been done.

This does not mean laptops are useless. Typed notes are easier to search, share and reorganise, and for students with certain disabilities a keyboard may be essential. Nor do the studies show that handwriting is magic. Their point is narrower: what helps learning is the effort of summarising, not the pen itself. The same studies found that when typists were simply told not to copy word for word, many of them carried on doing so, because the habit of transcribing is hard to break when the keyboard makes it so easy. A typist who deliberately writes short summaries in her own words, rather than transcribing, may gain much of the same benefit.

Laptops bring another risk that has nothing to do with typing speed. A screen opens the way to messages, shopping and videos, and a student who drifts to them misses parts of the lecture. Some studies have found that this also distracts the students sitting nearby, who can see the screen. Teachers who ban laptops usually mention this problem first, ahead of any argument about memory, because it is the one they can see from the front of the room every day.

The practical lesson is modest, and it applies well beyond the lecture hall. Whether they use a pen or a keyboard, students learn more when they treat note-taking as a way of thinking rather than as a way of recording. The tool matters less than the habit.

z1-rc4.title: Passage: The hidden price of free returns
z1-rc4.html:
Passage: The hidden price of free returns

Online shops discovered early that the biggest obstacle to selling clothes over the internet was not price but doubt. A customer who cannot touch a fabric or try on a jacket hesitates, and a hesitating customer closes the tab. Free returns removed that doubt at a stroke. If the jacket did not fit, it could go back at no cost, so the risk of buying shifted from the shopper to the shop. Sales rose, and for a while the policy looked like one of the cleverest bargains in retail, a small cost in exchange for a large and lasting change in habits.

The bargain, however, was never as free as its name. Every returned parcel must be collected, transported, inspected, cleaned or repackaged and put back into stock, and a fair share of it cannot be resold at full price at all. Fashion moves fast; a dress that comes back after three weeks may have missed its season. Some of it is sold off cheaply to discount traders, and some is simply destroyed, because sorting it costs more than it is worth. The shopper sees none of this. To her the return is a click and a trip to the post office.

The policy also changed how people shop. Customers began to order the same shirt in three sizes, intending from the start to send two back, a habit retailers call bracketing. What had been a safety net turned into a fitting room that happened to be located in the customer's bedroom, with the shop paying the rent. For businesses whose margins were already thin, returns quietly ate a large slice of the profit that the extra sales had seemed to promise.

Several large retailers have now begun to charge a small fee for returns, or to waive it only for members of a paid loyalty scheme. They have been careful to describe the change in environmental language, pointing to the lorries and the landfill, and the environmental case is real enough. But it would be naive to think that the motive is chiefly green. A fee that discourages bracketing protects margins first and the planet second.

None of this means free returns were a mistake. They did what they were designed to do: they persuaded millions of people to trust a new way of shopping. The difficulty is that a policy introduced to overcome a temporary doubt became a permanent expectation, and expectations are much harder to withdraw than to create.

z1-rc5.title: Passage: What a city tree is worth
z1-rc5.html:
Passage: What a city tree is worth

Ask a city council why it plants trees and you will usually hear a list of services: shade that cools the street, leaves that trap dust, roots that soak up storm water, and branches that give birds somewhere to live. Each of these benefits can be measured, and some cities now publish reports that put a money value on their trees, adding up the electricity saved on air-conditioning and the drainage costs avoided. The totals are impressive, often running into large sums for a single city, and they have helped tree budgets survive in years when other spending was cut.

There is a risk in this way of arguing, however. Once a tree is defended as a service provider, it can be judged like any other provider, and replaced if a cheaper one appears. A drainage engineer may point out that an underground tank handles storm water more reliably than roots. A shade sail is cheaper to install than a tree is to raise. On a narrow spreadsheet, the tree begins to lose.

The spreadsheet also struggles with time. A newly planted sapling provides almost none of the listed services; a mature tree provides them in abundance. The value of the young tree lies almost entirely in a future that the yearly budget does not see. When money is short, it is tempting to cut the maintenance that keeps saplings alive, since the loss will not show up in the accounts for decades. Many cities have planted generously and then watched a large share of their new trees die within a few years.

None of this is an argument against measurement. Numbers have rescued many trees, and a council that knows how much its canopy is worth makes better decisions than one that does not. The point is that the numbers capture only the part of a tree's value that resembles a utility. People also value trees for reasons that resist pricing: the sense of seasons changing on an ordinary street, the memory of a particular tree outside a childhood home, the feeling that a neighbourhood is cared for. These are not soft extras, to be mentioned once the serious accounting is done. They are often what residents mention first when a tree is threatened.

A sensible policy would use the numbers as a floor rather than a ceiling, a minimum case that any tree can make for itself, while leaving room for the reasons that cannot be counted.

questions.question: What problem does the first paragraph describe?
questions.solution: Paragraph 1 says the average drill is used for only a few minutes, and the same is true of ladders, tents and so on: households buy items they hardly use. Option 1 is not claimed (items are thrown away 'while it still works'). Options 3 and 4 are never said.
options: Tools sold today break much sooner than older tools did.
Many households buy equipment that they use very rarely.
Families do not know how to use the tools they own.
Shops do not stock enough tools for city flats.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT mentioned as a benefit of a library of things?
questions.solution: Paragraph 3 lists money, space and waste. Volunteers appear in the passage, but creating jobs is never presented as a benefit (volunteers are unpaid in any case).
options: Saving money
Saving storage space
Reducing waste
Creating jobs for volunteers

questions.question: According to the passage, why did several early projects close?
questions.solution: Paragraph 4: 'If borrowers return items late or broken, the collection shrinks and members drift away. Several early projects closed for exactly this reason.' The other options are not given as reasons.
options: They could not find enough donated tools.
Borrowers returned items late or damaged, and members drifted away.
Members preferred to buy their own tools.
The yearly fee was too high for most families.

questions.question: The author compares a shelf of shared tools to a town square in order to suggest that
questions.solution: The last paragraph says members value meeting neighbours, and the comparison is explained directly: 'it gives people a reason to meet.' Option 1 takes the comparison literally; options 3 and 4 are not said.
options: libraries of things should be built in town squares.
the libraries give neighbours a reason to meet and get to know each other.
town squares are no longer useful in modern cities.
tools were once sold in town squares.

questions.question:
The four sentences below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Enter the sequence of the four numbers (e.g. 2143).

  1. Instead, it quietly stores up heat during the day and releases it slowly through the night.
  2. A stone wall facing the sun behaves very differently from a thin metal sheet.
  3. The metal sheet heats up quickly at noon but loses its warmth almost as soon as the sun sets.
  4. This is why old houses with thick walls feel cool in the afternoon and warm late in the evening.
questions.solution: Correct order 2314. 2 introduces the contrast between a stone wall and a metal sheet. 3 describes the metal sheet. 1 ('Instead, it…') returns to the stone wall in contrast with the sheet. 4 ('This is why…') draws the everyday consequence.

questions.question:
The four sentences below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Enter the sequence of the four numbers (e.g. 2143).

  1. The result was a map that looked strange but saved countless lives.
  2. Before such maps, people simply took the closest route on paper, even when it crossed rough water.
  3. Sailors had long noticed that the shortest path between two ports was not always the safest one.
  4. So a few chart-makers began to mark currents, reefs and seasonal storms alongside distances.
questions.solution: Correct order 3241. 3 states the observation. 2 explains what people did before (took the shortest paper route). 4 ('So…') gives the response. 1 ('The result…') concludes.

questions.question:
Five jumbled sentences related to a topic are given below. Four of them can be put together to form a coherent paragraph. Identify the odd one out and key in its number.

  1. Many people think of sleep as time when the brain switches off.
  2. In fact, several kinds of activity continue and even increase during sleep.
  3. Some of this activity appears to help the brain sort and store what was learned during the day.
  4. Mattresses filled with foam became popular in the late twentieth century.
  5. Losing sleep before an exam may therefore cost more than it gains.
questions.solution: Sentences 1, 2, 3 and 5 argue that the sleeping brain is active and that this helps memory, so cutting sleep before an exam is unwise. Sentence 4, about mattresses, is off-topic.

questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Farmers in dry regions once dug small pits in their fields and filled them with crop waste before planting. When rain came, the pits caught water and the rotting waste fed the soil around them. The method fell out of use when chemical fertiliser became cheap, but in recent years some farmers have returned to it, finding that it helps their crops survive long dry spells at very little cost.
questions.solution: Option 2 keeps the method, what it does and why it is being revived. Option 1 overstates the role of fertiliser. Option 3 turns a description into a command. Option 4 is a claim the paragraph does not make.
options: Chemical fertiliser has ruined farming in dry regions.
An old, low-cost method of catching water and enriching soil is being revived because it helps crops survive dry spells.
Farmers should dig pits in every field before planting.
Crop waste is the best fertiliser available today.

questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Children who are praised for being clever often become cautious. Afraid of losing the label, they avoid hard problems that might expose them. Children praised for their effort, by contrast, tend to choose harder tasks, because failing at a hard task does not threaten the way they see themselves. The kind of praise we give therefore shapes not only how children feel but which challenges they are willing to take on.
questions.solution: Option 2 captures the contrast and its effect. Option 1 contradicts the paragraph. Option 3 overgeneralises ('always'). Option 4 goes beyond what is said.
options: Children should never be praised.
Praising effort rather than cleverness makes children more willing to attempt hard tasks.
Clever children always avoid difficult problems.
Effort matters more than talent in every field.

questions.question:
There is a sentence or phrase missing in the paragraph below. Read the paragraph and choose the option that best completes it.

Street vendors in many cities sell cut fruit from carts. Buyers like the convenience, and vendors earn a living with little investment. ____ Some cities have responded by giving vendors simple training and clean water points, rather than banning the carts.
questions.solution: The final sentence describes a response (training, clean water) to a problem. Only option 2 supplies that problem: hygiene. The other options do not explain why a response was needed.
options: Fruit is healthier than most packaged snacks.
But fruit left uncovered in heat and dust can make people ill.
Many vendors come from villages near the city.
Carts are cheaper to buy than shops.

questions.question: According to the passage, how do bees produce heat in cold weather?
questions.solution: Paragraph 2 says it directly: they produce heat 'by rapidly tensing the large flight muscles … without moving their wings'. The other options are not mentioned.
options: By flying in circles inside the hive.
By tensing their flight muscles rapidly without moving their wings.
By eating more honey than usual.
By sealing the hive entrance with wax.

questions.question: Why does the passage mention a damp cloth around a clay pot?
questions.solution: Paragraph 3 compares the bees' water-spreading to a damp cloth: 'Evaporation takes heat away, so the hive is cooled in roughly the way…'. It is an analogy for the cooling mechanism, not a literal practice.
options: To show that bees build hives from clay.
To explain that evaporation of water carries heat away, which cools the hive.
To suggest that beekeepers should wrap hives in cloth.
To show that bees need water to make honey.

questions.question: What can be inferred about why the colony's response to temperature changes is smooth?
questions.solution: Paragraph 4: no bee is in charge, individuals differ slightly in their trigger temperatures, so 'a few bees respond first, then more join in'. Option 1 contradicts 'No single bee is in charge'.
options: One senior bee decides when the colony should heat or cool.
Individual bees start to fan or shiver at slightly different temperatures, so they join in gradually.
Bees only respond to temperature at night.
The hive's wax walls keep the temperature fixed.

questions.question: Which statement best expresses the author's view in the last paragraph?
questions.solution: The last sentence: 'Good management … means making the bees' own work easier rather than replacing it.' Option 1 is the opposite; option 3 contradicts the example; option 4 is not said.
options: Beekeepers should control hive temperature with heaters and fans.
Good beekeeping supports the colony's own temperature control rather than replacing it.
Hives should always be opened in the morning.
Bees cannot survive without beekeepers.

questions.question:
The four sentences below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Enter the sequence of the four numbers (e.g. 2143).

  1. Within a week, however, he noticed that customers stayed longer and bought more.
  2. A bookshop in a busy street once replaced its bright white lights with softer, warmer lamps.
  3. Its owner had expected the change only to cut his electricity bill.
  4. He has never gone back to the old lights.
questions.solution: Correct order 2314. 2 introduces the change. 3 gives the owner's expectation. 1 ('however') contrasts it with what actually happened. 4 is the closing outcome. Hence 2314.

questions.question:
The four sentences below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Enter the sequence of the four numbers (e.g. 2143).

  1. These readable marks let later researchers see how the river's floods had changed over centuries.
  2. For hundreds of years, officials in the town carved the height of each flood on a stone pillar by the river.
  3. Without the pillar, such a long record would have been impossible to rebuild.
  4. Some marks have faded, but most can still be read.
questions.solution: Correct order 2413. 2 introduces the pillar. 4 describes the state of the marks. 1 ('These records…') explains their use. 3 concludes by stressing the pillar's value.

questions.question:
Five jumbled sentences related to a topic are given below. Four of them can be put together to form a coherent paragraph. Identify the odd one out and key in its number.

  1. Learning a musical instrument takes regular, patient practice.
  2. Short daily sessions usually work better than one long session a week.
  3. Piano keys were once made from ivory.
  4. Practising slowly at first helps the fingers learn the right movements.
  5. Over months, these small habits add up to real skill.
questions.solution: Sentences 1, 2, 4 and 5 give advice about how to practise and why it works. Sentence 3, about ivory piano keys, does not fit.

questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Many cities planted a single kind of tree along entire avenues because it grew fast and looked neat. When a disease arrived that attacked that species, whole streets lost their trees within a few years. Planners now prefer to mix several species on each street, so that one pest or disease cannot strip a neighbourhood bare.
questions.solution: Option 2 states the lesson and the reason. Option 1 overgeneralises. Option 3 is not claimed. Option 4 contradicts the paragraph.
options: Fast-growing trees are always a poor choice for cities.
Planting many species instead of one protects city streets from losing all their trees to a single disease.
Tree diseases are spreading faster than ever before.
Planners no longer plant trees along avenues.

questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

A traveller who learns a few phrases of the local language is often treated more warmly, even if the phrases are spoken badly. The effort itself signals respect. Locals tend to respond by slowing down, using simpler words or switching to the traveller's language, so the attempt makes communication easier rather than harder.
questions.solution: Option 2 keeps both points: effort earns warmth and helps communication. Option 1 is not required by the paragraph. Option 3 overstates one possible response. Option 4 contradicts it.
options: Travellers should become fluent before visiting a country.
Even a small, imperfect effort to speak the local language earns goodwill and eases communication.
Locals always prefer to speak the traveller's language.
Speaking a language badly is disrespectful.

questions.question:
There is a sentence or phrase missing in the paragraph below. Read the paragraph and choose the option that best completes it.

Mobile phone screens have grown larger almost every year. Larger screens make videos and maps easier to see. ____ This is why some manufacturers have started selling smaller models again, aimed at people who value comfort over size.
questions.solution: The last sentence says smaller models appeal to people who value comfort. Option 2 supplies the problem with large screens that explains this. The others support big screens or are unrelated.
options: Phone batteries have also improved.
However, very large phones can be awkward to hold and use with one hand.
Many people now watch films on their phones.
Maps on phones are more accurate than paper maps.

questions.question: What is the 'clear win for the laptop' that the first paragraph describes?
questions.solution: Paragraph 1: typists can type almost as fast as the teacher speaks, so 'more words captured should mean more material to revise from'. Option 2 is what the studies question, not the apparent win.
options: Laptops let students capture more of the lecture's words.
Laptops make students understand lectures better.
Laptops are cheaper than notebooks.
Teachers prefer students who type.

questions.question: According to the passage, why might handwriting help understanding?
questions.solution: Paragraph 2: because a hand-writer cannot copy everything, 'she has to decide what matters and put it in her own words', which makes her think about the ideas. Option 1 is a benefit of typed notes.
options: Handwritten notes are easier to search later.
Writing slowly forces students to choose and rephrase the important ideas.
Pens are less distracting than laptops for nearby students.
Teachers speak more slowly when students write by hand.

questions.question: Which of the following would the author most likely agree with?
questions.solution: Paragraph 3 says the benefit comes from summarising, not the pen, and 'a typist who deliberately writes short summaries … may gain much of the same benefit'. Option 3 is explicitly rejected ('Nor … handwriting is magic'). Options 1 and 4 go against the passage.
options: All students should be banned from using laptops in class.
A typist who writes brief summaries in her own words can learn as effectively as a hand-writer.
Handwriting has a special effect on the brain that typing can never match.
Longer notes always lead to better marks.

questions.question: The fourth paragraph mainly discusses
questions.solution: Paragraph 4 is about distraction: messages, shopping and videos, which also affect students who can see the screen.
options: how fast students can type.
the risk that laptops distract both their users and the students nearby.
why typed notes are easier to share.
how teachers should give lectures.

questions.question:
The four sentences below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Enter the sequence of the four numbers (e.g. 2143).

  1. As a result, a single bad storm can wipe out the whole supply for a season.
  2. Most of the world's vanilla comes from a small number of growing regions.
  3. These regions also lie in the path of tropical cyclones.
  4. That is one reason the price of vanilla jumps so sharply from year to year.
questions.solution: Correct order 2314. 2 introduces the concentration of supply. 3 ('These regions…') adds the cyclone risk. 1 ('As a result…') gives the consequence. 4 links it to price swings.

questions.question:
The four sentences below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Enter the sequence of the four numbers (e.g. 2143).

  1. Then, as the queue grew, they added a second counter and a numbered token system.
  2. At first, the clinic had one counter where patients both registered and paid.
  3. The tokens meant patients could sit down instead of standing in line.
  4. Waiting times fell by almost half within a month.
questions.solution: Correct order 2134. 2 describes the starting point ('At first'). 1 ('Then…') describes the change. 3 explains the effect of tokens. 4 reports the overall result.

questions.question:
Five jumbled sentences related to a topic are given below. Four of them can be put together to form a coherent paragraph. Identify the odd one out and key in its number.

  1. Glass bottles can be washed and refilled many times.
  2. Some dairies collect empty bottles from customers' doorsteps.
  3. Each refill saves the energy needed to make a new bottle.
  4. Cows produce more milk in spring than in winter.
  5. This simple loop can cut packaging waste sharply.
questions.solution: Sentences 1, 2, 3 and 5 describe a refill system for bottles and its benefit. Sentence 4, about seasonal milk yields, is unrelated to packaging.

questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

In many offices, meetings are scheduled for a full hour simply because calendars default to that length. Work then expands to fill the time. Teams that switch the default to 25 or 50 minutes often find they cover the same ground, and the short break between meetings lets people prepare or rest.
questions.solution: Option 2 has the cause (defaults) and the fix (shorter defaults, same ground covered). Option 1 is extreme. Option 3 is a narrow reading. Option 4 is a side benefit, not the main point.
options: Meetings should be banned in offices.
Default meeting lengths make meetings longer than needed; shorter defaults save time without losing content.
Calendars are badly designed.
People need longer breaks between meetings.

questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Old buildings are often torn down because repairing them looks expensive. But demolition and new construction use large amounts of energy and materials, much of it hidden in the making of cement and steel. When these hidden costs are counted, repairing and reusing an old building is frequently the cheaper choice for the environment.
questions.solution: Option 2 states the argument with its key reason. Option 1 is not discussed. Option 3 is extreme. Option 4 confuses environmental cost with money and adds 'always'.
options: Old buildings are more beautiful than new ones.
Counting the hidden energy and materials of new construction often makes reusing old buildings the better environmental choice.
Cement and steel should not be used in construction.
Repairing old buildings is always cheaper in money terms.

questions.question:
There is a sentence or phrase missing in the paragraph below. Read the paragraph and choose the option that best completes it.

Many people try to learn a new skill by watching hours of videos. Watching feels productive because the steps look easy on screen. ____ That is why teachers of cooking, music and sport insist that students practise each step themselves, even clumsily, from the very first day.
questions.solution: The last sentence says teachers insist on practice from day one. Option 2 gives the reason: watching does not build the skill. The other options do not lead to that conclusion.
options: Videos are often longer than they need to be.
But the hands and body learn only by doing, and watching alone rarely builds the skill.
Many videos are available free of charge.
Some teachers also make their own videos.

questions.question: According to the passage, why did free returns initially boost online clothing sales?
questions.solution: Paragraph 1: the obstacle was doubt; with free returns 'the risk of buying shifted from the shopper to the shop', so hesitation disappeared and sales rose. None of the other options is stated.
options: They allowed shops to raise prices without losing customers.
They shifted the risk of a poor fit from the buyer to the seller, removing customers' hesitation.
They reduced the cost of transporting parcels.
They encouraged shoppers to visit physical stores.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards retailers' environmental explanation for return fees is best described as
questions.solution: Paragraph 4 grants that 'the environmental case is real enough' but says 'it would be naive to think that the motive is chiefly green' and that the fee 'protects margins first'. That is scepticism, not dismissal (option 2 contradicts 'real enough') or acceptance.
options: wholehearted acceptance.
complete dismissal, since returns have no environmental cost.
sceptical: the environmental case is real, but profit is the main motive.
indifferent: the author takes no position.

questions.question: The phrase 'a fitting room that happened to be located in the customer's bedroom, with the shop paying the rent' suggests that
questions.solution: The metaphor follows the description of bracketing: ordering several sizes intending to return most. The shop bears the cost ('paying the rent'). The other options read the metaphor literally or miss its point.
options: shops have begun renting rooms in customers' homes.
customers now use home deliveries to try on clothes they never intended to keep, at the shop's expense.
customers prefer shopping from bed.
fitting rooms in stores have become too expensive to run.

questions.question: Which of the following best captures the point of the final paragraph?
questions.solution: The paragraph says free returns 'did what they were designed to do' but turned a temporary measure into 'a permanent expectation', which is hard to withdraw. Option 4 contradicts 'None of this means free returns were a mistake'.
options: Free returns should be abolished immediately.
Free returns achieved their purpose, but once customers came to expect them, they became hard to withdraw.
Customers no longer trust online shopping.
Retailers made a serious mistake in offering free returns.

questions.question:
The four sentences below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Enter the sequence of the four numbers (e.g. 2143).

  1. What looks like indecision is often a rational response to that uncertainty.
  2. Investors facing an unclear future frequently hold large amounts of cash rather than committing it.
  3. Critics call this hoarding and blame it for slow growth.
  4. Waiting is valuable when the cost of a wrong commitment is high and new information is expected soon.
questions.solution: Correct order 2314. 2 states the behaviour. 3 gives the critics' view ('this hoarding'). 1 counters it ('that uncertainty' refers back to 2's 'unclear future'). 4 explains why waiting can be rational. 1 must follow 3 because it rebuts the critics' description.

questions.question:
The four sentences below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Enter the sequence of the four numbers (e.g. 2143).

  1. Yet the same feature that makes them durable makes them a problem once they are thrown away.
  2. Plastics were prized for decades because they resist rot, water and most chemicals.
  3. In soil or sea they can persist for generations, breaking into ever smaller fragments.
  4. Designing materials that last exactly as long as they are needed has therefore become a serious research goal.
questions.solution: Correct order 2134. 2 introduces the valued property. 1 ('Yet the same feature…') turns it into a problem. 3 describes the problem. 4 ('therefore') draws the conclusion.

questions.question:
Five jumbled sentences related to a topic are given below. Four of them can be put together to form a coherent paragraph. Identify the odd one out and key in its number.

  1. A city's noise is rarely measured as carefully as its air.
  2. Yet constant traffic noise has been linked to poor sleep and raised stress.
  3. Quieter road surfaces and lower night-time speed limits can reduce it noticeably.
  4. Some musicians deliberately record city sounds for their compositions.
  5. Treating noise as a health issue, not just a nuisance, would change how roads are planned.
questions.solution: Sentences 1, 2, 3 and 5 build an argument that urban noise is a neglected health problem with practical remedies. Sentence 4, about musicians using city sounds, does not belong to that argument.

questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Translators are often told to be faithful to the original. But faithfulness to individual words can betray the meaning of the whole. A joke translated word for word stops being funny; a polite phrase becomes rude. The translator's real loyalty is to the effect the text has on its readers, and that sometimes requires departing from its exact words.
questions.solution: Option 2 states the thesis precisely. Option 1 exaggerates. Options 3 and 4 seize on examples and overgeneralise them.
options: Translators should ignore the original text.
Good translation is faithful to a text's effect on readers, which may require departing from its exact words.
Jokes cannot be translated.
Word-for-word translation is always rude.

questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Public parks are usually judged by their size, yet a small park that people can reach in five minutes may do more good than a large one at the edge of town. People visit what is close, and frequent short visits contribute more to health and community life than an occasional trip to a distant green space.
questions.solution: Option 2 has the claim and the reason. Option 1 is extreme. Option 3 is not argued. Option 4 misstates the point (distance reduces frequency; enjoyment is not discussed).
options: Large parks are a waste of land.
Closeness matters more than size in judging a park's value, because frequent short visits do more good.
Every city should build more parks.
People do not enjoy visiting distant parks.

questions.question:
There is a sentence or phrase missing in the paragraph below. Read the paragraph and choose the option that best completes it.

Many companies reward staff for the number of ideas they submit to a suggestion scheme. The result is predictable. ____ A better approach is to reward ideas that are actually tested, whatever their outcome, so that quality rather than quantity is encouraged.
questions.solution: The 'predictable' result of rewarding quantity, which the last sentence sets out to fix ('quality rather than quantity'), is a flood of low-quality ideas: option 2. The other options do not describe a problem caused by counting ideas.
options: Employees enjoy being asked for their opinions.
The scheme fills with small, hasty proposals that no one has the time to evaluate.
Most companies do not have a suggestion scheme.
Ideas are the lifeblood of every organisation.

questions.question: The author's main concern about valuing trees by their services is that
questions.solution: Paragraph 2: once trees are defended as service providers they 'can be judged like any other provider, and replaced if a cheaper one appears' (tanks, shade sails). Option 1 contradicts 'Each of these benefits can be measured'.
options: the services of trees are too difficult to measure.
it invites replacing trees with cheaper alternatives that provide the same service.
it makes tree budgets too large.
it ignores the cost of planting trees.

questions.question: Why, according to the passage, do many newly planted city trees die?
questions.solution: Paragraph 3: the young tree's value is in the future, so when money is short it is tempting to cut sapling maintenance, and many new trees die. The other causes are not mentioned.
options: They are planted in unsuitable soil.
Maintenance for saplings is cut because their value lies in a future the yearly budget does not see.
Residents remove them because they block light.
Storm water damages their roots.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's argument in paragraph 2?
questions.solution: Paragraph 2 warns that service-based valuation leads to trees being replaced by cheaper substitutes. Evidence that cities using such valuations have not done so, and have planted more trees, directly undercuts that risk. Option 1 mildly helps trees but does not address the claimed tendency.
options: Underground tanks are expensive to maintain.
In practice, cities that publish money values for trees have planted more trees, not fewer, and have not replaced trees with engineered alternatives.
Shade sails are popular in hot countries.
Birds prefer old trees to young ones.

questions.question: What does the author mean by using the numbers 'as a floor rather than a ceiling'?
questions.solution: A floor is a minimum, a ceiling a maximum. The sentence adds 'a minimum case … while leaving room for the reasons that cannot be counted'. Option 1 treats the numbers as a ceiling, the opposite.
options: Trees should be valued only by their measurable services.
Measured services should set the minimum case for a tree, with unmeasurable values added on top.
Councils should spend as little as possible on trees.
Tree budgets should never be cut below a fixed level.

questions.question:
The four sentences below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Enter the sequence of the four numbers (e.g. 2143).

  1. That stability, rather than any single brilliant player, explained most of their success.
  2. Analysts studying a decade of results found that the most successful clubs were not those that spent the most on transfers.
  3. They were the ones that changed managers least often and kept a settled core of players.
  4. Spending still mattered, but only when it was combined with continuity.
questions.solution: Correct order 2314. 2 introduces the finding in negative form. 3 ('They were the ones…') completes it. 1 ('That stability…') interprets it. 4 qualifies the role of spending. 1 must follow 3 because 'That stability' refers to 3's settled managers and players.

questions.question:
The four sentences below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Enter the sequence of the four numbers (e.g. 2143).

  1. The second group, given no such instruction, remembered far less of it.
  2. In one experiment, two groups of volunteers read the same short story.
  3. One group was told beforehand that they would have to explain the story to a child.
  4. Preparing to teach, it seems, changes the way we take information in.
questions.solution: Correct order 2314. 2 sets up the experiment. 3 describes the first group's instruction. 1 ('The second group, given no such instruction') contrasts with 3. 4 draws the conclusion.

questions.question:
Five jumbled sentences related to a topic are given below. Four of them can be put together to form a coherent paragraph. Identify the odd one out and key in its number.

  1. Early weather forecasts relied heavily on the experience of individual forecasters.
  2. Modern forecasts are built from computer models that simulate the atmosphere.
  3. Forecasters still add judgement, especially for local effects that models handle poorly.
  4. Barometers measure air pressure using a column of liquid or a sealed metal box.
  5. The best forecasts today come from combining models with that human judgement.
questions.solution: Sentences 1, 2, 3 and 5 trace forecasting from personal experience to models plus judgement. Sentence 4 describes how barometers work, a technical detail outside that thread.

questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Warnings on products are meant to protect consumers, but when every product carries a long list of them, people stop reading. A warning about a genuine danger is then lost among warnings about trivial ones. Fewer, sharper warnings would therefore protect people better than the current flood.
questions.solution: Option 2 has the problem (dilution) and the proposed fix. Option 1 is extreme. Option 3 blames consumers, which the paragraph does not do. Option 4 introduces a motive not discussed.
options: Products should carry no warnings at all.
Too many warnings dilute attention, so fewer and clearer warnings would protect consumers better.
Consumers are careless about safety.
Manufacturers add warnings mainly to avoid lawsuits.

questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

A language's grammar is often taught as a set of rules handed down from authority. In fact most grammatical rules began as descriptions of how people already spoke. Over time, some descriptions hardened into commands, and the usage that had produced them moved on, leaving rules that describe how no one now speaks.
questions.solution: Option 2 traces the whole process the paragraph describes. Options 1 and 3 overstate. Option 4 contradicts the paragraph.
options: Grammar rules are useless.
Many grammar rules started as descriptions of usage, hardened into commands, and fell out of step as usage changed.
People should speak as they please.
Grammar is invented by authorities.

questions.question:
There is a sentence or phrase missing in the paragraph below. Read the paragraph and choose the option that best completes it.

A town introduced a fine for parents who arrived late to collect their children from a day-care centre. To the town's surprise, late arrivals increased. ____ Removing the fine later did not restore the old behaviour, because the sense of obligation had already been replaced by a price.
questions.solution: The last sentence says the 'sense of obligation had already been replaced by a price'. Option 2 supplies exactly that mechanism. Option 1 could explain no change but not the replacement of obligation by price.
options: The fine was too small to matter to most parents.
Parents seemed to treat the fine as a fee for extra time, which relieved them of the guilt they had felt before.
Many parents worked longer hours that year.
The day-care staff did not enforce the fine.
